summary: Records an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society allowing Sun's Network File System specifications to enter the IETF standards process, covering the NFS version 4 work.

eli5.summary: A written deal where a company agreed to let the internet's rule makers take over and improve its file sharing rules.

questions: what is the 24 month limit in the nfs agreement
subtitle: The agreement that let the IETF take Sun's NFS specifications and develop NFS version 4.

tldr.problem: Sun owned the NFS specifications, and the IETF needed rights to use and change them to develop NFS version 4 as an Internet standard.
tldr.mechanism: Sun grants the Internet Society, including the IETF, a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license solely to make the specification an Internet standard, and agrees not to license anyone else to evolve it as a standard.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is not a standard, only the public record of the agreement. The evolution license ends if the specification is not a Proposed Standard within 24 months of signing.

today: RFC 2339 is an Informational record of a 1998 agreement, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a legal record, not a technical specification.

sections.title: What the Agreement Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2339 records an agreement dated 3 March 1998 between Sun Microsystems (the "Donor") and the Internet Society, which includes the IETF. The RFC says it is not a standard but an official public record. It lets Sun's Network File System specifications flow into the IETF Standards process.

The referenced RFC 1094 (NFS, March 1989) and RFC 1813 (NFS Version 3, June 1995) are incorporated by reference. Exhibit A defines the specification as those two RFCs minus the portions that assume NFS runs over XDR and ONC RPC, plus control of ONC RPC program number 100003 (NFS) for generating version numbers 4 and onward.
sections.eli5: It is the signed paper saying the Internet group may take Sun's file sharing rules and build the next version.

sections.title: The Licenses
sections.content:
Section 1 grants a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license under Sun copyrights, essential Sun patent rights and other Sun intellectual property to use, reproduce, distribute, perform, display and make derivative works of the specification. Section 2 limits it to the sole purpose of seeking to make the specification an Internet standard.

Section 3 lets the Licensees evolve and modify the specification through the Internet Standardization Process (RFC 2026). Sun may not license any other party, including another standards group, to evolve, modify or promote the specification as a standard. Sun's own work outside the process must be labeled a non-standard development and must not refer to the Internet Standards Process.
sections.eli5: Sun lets the Internet group use and change the rules for free, and promises not to give the same job to anyone else.

sections.title: Future Licenses and the 24-Month Limit
sections.content:
The Licensees have no duty to publish the specification or take it onto the standards track, and no obligation of confidentiality. Sun represents that, to its knowledge, there are no infringement claims against it.

If the specification reaches Proposed Standard within 24 months of the agreement, Sun will license it to others at no charge on substantially similar terms, so long as they implement and comply with the standard. If not, the license granted in Section 3 terminates.

The note under Exhibit A observes that ISOC already has a license to XDR and ONC RPC (RFC 1790), so it may decide whether NFS Version 4 uses them.
sections.eli5: If the new rules become official within two years, everyone may use them for free. If not, the Internet group loses its right to change them.

sections.title: Disclaimers and Security
sections.content:
The specification is provided "as is" with warranties disclaimed and Sun's liability excluded. The agreement is the entire agreement between the parties, changes need signed writing, and California law applies where no U.S. federal law governs. It was signed by Rich Green for Sun on 3 March 1998 and by Donald M. Heath for the Internet Society on 6 March 1998.

On security, the RFC says it records an agreement rather than describing a technology, so security is not directly affected, but one aim of an IETF NFS working group should be adequate security in a standards track NFS protocol.
sections.eli5: Like most contracts, it says Sun is not to blame if something goes wrong. It also reminds everyone that the new file sharing rules should be safe.
